evals.prompt: Define April Dunford-style product positioning in 2-3 sentences. Include competitive alternatives, differentiated value, best-fit customers, and market category.
expected_elements: Explains positioning as market-context design or choosing context for product value
Starts from customer-real competitive alternatives
Connects unique attributes to differentiated value
Names best-fit customers or customers who care most
Names market category or frame of reference
Does not define positioning as a tagline or brand slogan

evals.prompt: Explain the mental model of Dunford positioning. Name at least 6 primitives and describe how they connect in sequence.
expected_elements: At least 6 of: competitive alternatives, unique attributes, value themes, best-fit customers, market category, trend context, proof, captured position, sales narrative
Explains that alternatives come before attributes
Explains that attributes must map to customer value
Explains that target customers and category depend on the value evidence
Explains that the output aligns go-to-market teams

evals.prompt: Why does this positioning skill exist for agents? Name the failure modes it prevents.
expected_elements: Prevents treating positioning as tagline writing
Prevents company-internal competitor lists
Prevents differentiation without buyer value
Prevents broad category choice that hides advantage
Prevents trend hype before value and category are clear

evals.prompt: Distinguish positioning from Playing to Win, Blue Ocean Strategy, Porter's Five Forces, Seven Powers, and microcopy. Give a mechanism-level reason each neighbor is different.
expected_elements: Playing to Win formulates integrated strategy choices
Blue Ocean Strategy reconstructs value curves and market boundaries
Porter's Five Forces diagnoses industry structure and profit pressure
Seven Powers classifies durable moat mechanisms
Microcopy writes finished wording after the position is chosen
Positioning chooses the product-market context that makes differentiated value obvious

evals.prompt: Place Dunford positioning among strategy and go-to-market frameworks. What upstream inputs can feed it, and what downstream outputs can follow it?
expected_elements: Classifies it as product positioning or go-to-market strategy method
Names upstream inputs such as customer research, win/loss, sales calls, alternatives, or product attributes
Names downstream outputs such as sales deck, website messaging, demo flow, category choice, or product-marketing narrative
Keeps it distinct from full company strategy and final copywriting

evals.prompt: Give an analogy for positioning that preserves category framing and customer-relative alternatives. Then name one bad analogy and explain what it gets wrong.
expected_elements: Uses an analogy involving shelf placement, map placement, frame of reference, or comparison context
Maps alternatives to comparison set
Maps category to the context that creates buyer expectations
Rejects a bad analogy that treats positioning as decoration, slogan writing, or pure persuasion

evals.prompt: Novel scenario: A startup says its positioning is "the AI platform for modern teams". Buyers actually compare it with spreadsheets and weekly status meetings. Apply Dunford positioning by diagnosing what is missing and proposing a better next analysis step.
expected_elements: Rejects the generic AI-platform claim as insufficient
Starts from spreadsheets and status meetings as competitive alternatives
Asks for unique attributes relative to those alternatives
Maps attributes to buyer value themes
Identifies which customers care most
Tests market category before writing final copy
Labels assumptions rather than inventing certainty
